speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: and as he does so,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: he can also offer amendments that have nothing to do with that bill,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: each of which can stall the bill even further.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A unanimous consent agreement sets those freedoms aside It fixes the allotted time
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: for debate and constrains the opportunity to amend it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Earlier leaders had rarely used such agreements,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: and even when they had,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: they'd only used them after weeks of debate on a bill
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: that had already been exhausted in its deliberations.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Johnson made their use the norm in the Senate.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: He wouldn't even allow a bill to reach the floor until such an agreement was in place.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And the reason was that Johnson wanted to control which bills reached the floor and
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: to keep the floor from changing anybody's mind.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: He wanted every vote settled in private beforehand,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: through the wheeling and dealing where his leverage worked best.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The last thing he wanted was for a long public debate about the merits of some bill
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: to change a senator's mind at the very last minute,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: or for a surprise amendment to unravel a deal
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: that he had spent weeks painstakingly brokering.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As Senator Paul Douglas put it,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: under Johnson, all the actions take place offstage before the play begins.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And the third tactic that Johnson employed was brokering all the deals to his advantage.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Johnson made sure that as much of the Senate's information as possible ran
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: through He had every committee assign a staffer to tell him what was being drafted.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And what he would and wouldn't give up to get it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In any session, the Senate faces hundreds of possible bills and amendments.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A senator's vote on one bill can be traded for another senator's vote on a different one.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And any single bill can be amended a dozen different ways to win somebody over.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So there's almost an endless combination of possible deals to be made.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Johnson made sure that he was the one instigating and brokering most of these deals.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As a result, he would be making sure that any deal left Johnson coming out ahead.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A good example is how he got the Civil Rights Act of 1957 passed through the Senate.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Johnson was desperate to make sure that at least some civil rights bill passed
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: that year, even if it was weak.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That's because he wanted to become president,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: but no Southerner with his record of consistently voting
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: against civil rights could hope to win the Democratic presidential nomination
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The problem was there seemed to be no bill strong enough to win
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: the Northern liberals, yet weak enough that the Southerners wouldn't filibuster it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The sticking point was who would preside over the court cases
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: where Southern electoral officials were accused
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: of suppressing Black Southern senators insisted on jury trials,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: but Northern senators were livid because in their view,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: this would gut the whole bill.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The entire point of the law was to combat the exclusion of Black citizens from the voting rolls.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But Southern states required jurors to be registered voters.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And an all-white Southern jury would never convict a white registrar
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: for turning away Black voters.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And so any version that one side could accept, the other would reject.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A less creative legislator would have backed down.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But over the course of seven months,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Johnson built a masterful deal that brought together wholly unrelated factions and
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: whose byproduct included the passage of this civil rights law.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Midwestern senators got a vote on a federal dam that they had wanted for years
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: between Idaho and Oregon.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Midwestern Republicans,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: who had powerful railroad unions in their state,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: got a right to a jury trial extended to striking workers.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And moderates got a clause guaranteeing that black citizens
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Meanwhile,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: the jury trial guarantee for Southern election officials stayed in,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: which kept the bill weak enough that Southerners agreed not to filibuster it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A dam in Idaho and protections for union workers and federal jury rules had nothing
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: to do with voting rights in the South,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: at least not to anyone who lacked the inside knowledge and political creativity
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: of Lyndon Johnson.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Caro's books are the best written accounts of how political power actually works,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: but they are written so compellingly and with characters more vivid
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: and stories more gripping than any novel that it's very easy to get so engrossed
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: that you just keep turning the pages.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And you never stop and ask yourself,
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: what are the lessons these stories are teaching about power?

speaker: SPEAKER_00
